title: Naaman: The Healing of an Outsider
lead: God’s grace is not limited by nationality, religion, or social standing.
questions: Whose voice have you ignored simply because it belonged to someone of lower rank?
What chariot do you find it hard to step down from: what kind of rescue seems too simple for you, or beneath your station?
Has being close to holy things become your job, and how would you recognize Gehazi’s heart in yourself?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: The first verse of this story is astonishing: Naaman, commander of the army of enemy Aram, was highly regarded, “for through him the LORD had given victory to Aram.” The God of Israel was giving victory to the enemy’s army. Right after that we read: “And he was a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper.” Great, victorious, but. Many of us find ourselves in that verse: people with a respectable résumé and one “but” that only they know about. The chain of rescue begins with the person of lowest status: a young girl taken captive from Israel, a servant. She had every right to wish her master the worst, and instead she said, “If only my master would go to the prophet who is in Samaria.” In captivity she lost neither her identity nor her kindness. Just as astonishing: the grown-ups believed a child.

Elisha did not even come out to meet the general who had arrived with his whole retinue; through a messenger he told him to wash seven times in the Jordan. What flared up then was not the disease, but pride. Naaman had his own script for the healing, with a ceremony worthy of his rank, and what he got was a muddy river. “Are not the Abanah and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel?” They are. But grace cannot be received as a VIP client. Once again his subordinates saved him: if the prophet had told you to do some great thing, you would have done it; the only thing that offends you is how simple it is. Naaman stepped down from his chariot, dipped himself seven times, and his flesh “became like that of a little child.” He arrived as a general and came out of the water as a child. And he confessed: “Now I know for sure that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel.”

Elisha refused payment, because grace is not for sale. When the new convert asked about the bowing in the temple of Rimmon that his duties would force on him, the prophet answered: “Go in peace.” Young faith must not be crushed under burdens. The shadow in this story falls elsewhere: Gehazi, the prophet’s servant, ran after the refused silver, and Naaman’s leprosy clung to him. The foreigner left with faith, the insider with the disease. Nearness to the altar does not save by radiation. Jesus will recall Naaman in Nazareth, and His listeners will be filled with rage: grace does not respect the borders we patrol.

The first verse of this story should stop every reader of the Bible in their tracks: Naaman, commander of the army of Aram, was highly regarded, “for through him the LORD had given victory to Aram.” The LORD, the God of Israel, was giving victories to the enemy’s army. The Israelite author wrote this down without batting an eye, as if he wanted to stress from the very threshold that the God of this book is not a tribal deity who works only for his own. The same verse holds one more striking piece of information: “And he was a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper.” Great, respected, victorious, but. The Hebrew word translated as leprosy covered various skin diseases, and Naaman was apparently not shut out of normal life, since he commanded an army and had access to the king. But he carried on his body something that all his standing could neither hide nor heal. A great many of us fit into that one verse: people with a respectable résumé and one “but” that only we know about.

sections.heading: The Girl Who Knew Who She Was
paragraphs: The chain of rescue for this great man begins with the person of the lowest possible status in that world: a child, a girl, a slave, a foreigner. Aramean raiding bands had carried her off from Israel; she served Naaman’s wife. She had every right to wish her master the worst. Instead she said, “If only my master would go to the prophet who is in Samaria, he would cure him of his leprosy.” Torn from her home, stripped of everything, she did not lose two things: the knowledge of who she was, and goodwill toward the people among whom she lived. Perhaps she was one of those seven thousand who stayed faithful to God in unfavorable circumstances, mentioned in yesterday’s story. No one evangelized her or mentored her. It was enough that in the home she had been torn from, she had come to know God well enough to know that He heals enemies too. And one more thing deserves emphasis: the grown-ups in this story believed a child. Naaman took her words to the king, who on that basis sent out an entire diplomatic mission. Rescue often enters a house through the servants’ entrance. We just have to be able to hear it.

sections.heading: Diplomacy Knocks on the Wrong Door
paragraphs: The machinery of state springs into action: a letter from king to king, ten talents of silver, six thousand shekels of gold, ten sets of clothing. In the world of that day, you paid gods and their people in advance to secure a favor, so Naaman sets off to pay for his healing. Meanwhile the king of Israel, seeing the letter, tears his clothes: “Am I God, killing and giving life, that this man expects me to cure a leper?” The great of this world turn out to be helpless before one sick man, and a ruler who long ago lost touch with the God of his own land sees in a request for a miracle nothing but a political provocation. Only Elisha saves the situation: “Please let the man come to me, and he will know that there is a prophet in Israel.” The address of rescue turns out to be different from the one diplomacy assumed. Not the palace, but the prophet’s house.

sections.heading: A Messenger Instead of the Host
paragraphs: Naaman pulls up in front of Elisha’s house “with his horses and chariots,” with his whole retinue and all his wealth. And Elisha does not even come out. This is not disrespect; it is teaching. Had the prophet come out with honors, performed a ceremony, and accepted payment, Naaman would have gone back to Damascus convinced he had bought a service from an unusually effective specialist. The healing is meant to teach him something more: grace is not a service, and it has no rate card for important clients. So instead of the host, a messenger comes out with instructions: “Go and wash yourself seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean.” And what flares up then is not the disease, but pride: “I thought that he would surely come out, stand and call on the name of the LORD his God, and wave his hand over the spot to cure my leprosy.” Naaman had his script for the healing ready, with a ceremony worthy of his rank: a personal reception, a solemn prayer, a gesture over the sore. Instead he got a message through a servant and an order to bathe in a muddy border river. “Are not the Abanah and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel?” They are, General. But the quality of the water is not the point. Grace has this about it: it cannot be received as a VIP client. You have to come like anyone else. Here his subordinates rescue him again; for the second time in this story, people of lower rank see more clearly than their master: “My father, if the prophet had told you to do some great thing, would you not have done it? How much more, then, when he tells you, ‘Wash and be cleansed’?” If the task had been heroic, he would have done it without hesitation. What offends him is its simplicity.

sections.heading: Seven Times
paragraphs: Naaman steps down from his chariot and does the hardest thing for a man of his stature: he listens. He “dipped himself in the Jordan seven times, according to the word of the man of God, and his flesh was restored and became like that of a little child.” Seven times, not once. The text does not say what happened after each dip. It only stresses that Naaman carried out the whole instruction, and then he was cleansed. So there is no point in adding what the story does not tell us. In the Bible, God’s great works are sometimes a process: on Mount Carmel Elijah sent his servant to look for a sign of rain seven times; Jesus heals a blind man in two stages. Whoever climbs out of the water after the third dip because “it isn’t working” will never learn what was planned for the seventh. The place of this bath is no accident either. The Jordan is a river of thresholds: Israel once crossed it into the Promised Land, and on its bank Elijah handed his ministry to Elisha. Now a foreigner passes through it, in an unusual direction: not from the desert into the land, but from paganism into faith. Centuries later John the Baptist will begin immersing people as a sign of a new beginning in the same river where Naaman took his healing bath. Flesh “like that of a little child” is more than dermatology: the man who arrived as a general with a caravan of gold comes out of the river like a child. And he says the most important sentence in the story: “Now I know for sure that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel.” A pagan from Damascus confesses a faith the king of Israel could not bring himself to hold.

sections.heading: A Gift Refused and a Load of Soil
paragraphs: Then comes a scene that must have amazed Naaman more than the healing. Elisha refuses payment: “As surely as the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will not accept it.” In Naaman’s world, gods and their functionaries were paid; religion was a system of services. The prophet’s refusal teaches him more about the nature of the LORD in one moment than many a lecture could: grace cannot be bought, because it is not for sale. Gratitude, yes; a transaction, no. So Naaman asks for something else: as much Israelite soil as a pair of mules can carry. This request can be understood in two ways. In that world people commonly believed that a god acted within his own territory; the Arameans said of Israel’s God, “Their gods are gods of the hills.” So perhaps the newly converted general still thinks in the old way: I will take a piece of the territory so that I can worship the LORD back home. But there is a second, more beautiful reading: Naaman now counts himself a member of the LORD’s people and symbolically receives his share of the inheritance, as if saying: from now on I belong to this land, even while living in that one. Either way, his theology is still childlike, full of simplifications. And that bothers neither God nor the prophet. Faith does not have to be mature to be real. It only has to be heading in the right direction. Naaman asks the question of a new convert returning to his old world: what will happen when my king leans on my arm in the temple of Rimmon and I have to bow down with him? Elisha’s answer is a model of pastoral wisdom: “Go in peace.” No rulebook for the road, no list of conditions. The prophet trusts that the God who began His work in this man will carry it on. Young faith must not be crushed under burdens it cannot carry.

sections.heading: The Shadow in This Story
paragraphs: The text set for today ends with “Go in peace,” but the story has a shadow we must not skip. Gehazi, Elisha’s servant, a man who lived day in and day out with the LORD’s prophet, watched all this and counted the losses: “Look, my master has spared this Aramean, Naaman, while not accepting what he brought.” He ran after the chariot, lied, took silver and clothing, and hid them away. And he heard: “the leprosy of Naaman will cling to you.” The foreigner went home with faith and clean skin, and the insider, raised at the prophet’s side, walked away with the disease the other man had been rid of. This is a warning addressed not to the world, but to us, people who move among holy things every day. Nearness to the altar does not make us immune to greed, nor does it save by radiation. You can carry the prophet’s bag and miss everything he knew about God.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: In His sermon at Nazareth, the same one in which He mentioned the widow of Zarephath, Jesus added a second sentence: “there were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet,” yet not one of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian. His listeners were filled with rage, because they understood Him perfectly: grace does not respect the borders we patrol. Three things follow from this story for us. First: listen to the little ones. Naaman’s rescue came through a young servant girl and through subordinates who dared to correct their master. A community where only the important have a voice cuts itself off from God’s promptings. Second: do not set ceremonial conditions for grace. God has the right to heal you in a way that does not suit your rank, and in a river you did not choose. Third: beware of Gehazi’s fate. Faith is not inherited by holding a position among holy things. And if you carry your own “but,” remember: the God of this story heals foreign generals, so your origins, your past, or your position are no obstacle to Him. The only obstacle is sometimes the chariot we refuse to step down from.
